A stub is something that is cut short, broken off, or left over — a small piece that remains after most of something is gone. Think of it as the leftover, the remnant, or the short blunt end of something that was once fuller or longer.

This core idea branches out into several related meanings, all of which share that same feeling of "a small, shortened piece."
1. A Physical Remnant (the most direct meaning)

When you use something up until very little of it is left, that tiny remaining piece is a stub.

  • After writing with a pencil for weeks, you're left with a pencil stub — a short, blunt piece barely worth holding.
  • After a candle has burned almost completely down, the small waxy remains at the bottom is a candle stub.
  • After smoking a cigarette, the short leftover piece that you extinguish is a cigarette stub (sometimes called a "butt").

The common thread: something that used to be whole and full has been used up, cut down, or broken, and what's left behind — that short, blunt, sometimes awkward leftover — is a stub.

The word also applies to things that were always short by nature, not just worn down. A tree branch that was cut close to the trunk and left as a short protruding bump is a stub. A short, broken tooth (or a baby tooth that's partially worn) is called a stub. A short, thick nail that's been hammered down almost flush — same idea.
2. A Stub as a Record or Counterfoil (the "kept piece" meaning)

Here, a stub is the small detachable portion of a larger document that you keep as proof or a record after the main part has been torn away or used.

Imagine a paper ticket for a concert. It has two parts connected along a perforated line: the main ticket (which gets taken at the door) and a smaller piece on one end. After an attendant rips off the main portion, you're left holding that smaller piece. That's your ticket stub. It's proof you attended. People often keep them as souvenirs.

The same logic applies to:

  • Check stub (or check counterfoil): In a checkbook, when you write a check and tear it out, the thin strip that stays behind in the book is the stub. You write on it what the check was for and the amount — it's your personal record.
  • Pay stub: The slip of paper (or digital document) you receive alongside your salary payment, showing the breakdown — your gross pay, taxes deducted, deductions, and net pay. Even if the payment itself goes directly into your bank account, the pay stub is your record of how that amount was calculated. This is one of the most common uses of the word in everyday life.
  • Receipt stub, lottery stub, etc. — same idea in different contexts.

The defining feature here: the stub is always the smaller, retained portion — it's what's left after the main piece is gone, and it functions as a record or reference.
3. A Stub in Computing and Software Development (the placeholder meaning)

In the world of programming and software, a stub takes on a slightly different but related meaning: it's a minimal, incomplete piece of code that stands in for something that hasn't been built yet — or that deliberately does nothing (or does the simplest possible thing).

Imagine a team of developers is building a large application. Developer A is writing one piece of the program, and that piece needs to call a function that Developer B is supposed to write. But Developer B hasn't written it yet. So Developer A creates a stub — a placeholder function with the right name and structure, but with an empty body or a simple fake response (like always returning zero, or always returning "success"). This lets Developer A keep working without being blocked.

In the same way, when you're testing software, you sometimes don't want to call the real version of a function (maybe it costs money, connects to a live database, or is slow). So instead, you use a stub — a simplified fake version that behaves in a controlled, predictable way just for the purposes of the test.

The connection to the other meanings is clear: just like a pencil stub is an incomplete, reduced version of a full pencil, or a ticket stub is the small remaining portion of a full ticket — a code stub is an incomplete, bare-minimum version of a full piece of code.
4. A Stub in Networking and APIs (a close cousin to the programming meaning)

In distributed computing and networking, a stub is a small piece of code on one side of a connection that acts as a representative or stand-in for a service located elsewhere (often on another machine or server).

For example: when your app makes a request to a remote server, your app itself doesn't know all the low-level details of how to communicate across the network. A stub handles that — it sits on your side, looks like a normal function you can call, but behind the scenes it packages your request and sends it over the network. The stub is your local representative for something that lives far away.

This is a narrower, more technical meaning, but the core idea holds: a stub is a small, reduced stand-in for something larger or more complex.

Every meaning of "stub" (as a noun) circles back to the same intuition:

Something that is short, reduced, or incomplete — either the remnant of something larger, a small piece kept after the whole is gone, or a simplified placeholder standing in for something more complete.

SituationWhat the stub is

Whether you're looking at the nub of a worn pencil, the slip in your wallet from last year's concert, the salary breakdown from your employer, or a placeholder function in a codebase — in every case, a stub is small, partial, and either what remains or what stands in.
A Quick Feel for the Word in Sentences

• "I found an old concert ticket stub at the bottom of my bag."
  • "The pay stub showed that a lot was deducted for taxes this month."
  • "The developer wrote a stub for the payment function until the real implementation was ready."
  • "All that was left of the candle was a small wax stub."
  • "He stubbed his toe on the door — wait, that's the verb. As a noun: the broken, blunt stub of the old fence post jutted out from the ground."

The word carries a slight connotation of incompleteness or inadequacy. A stub is never the full thing — it's always the lesser, shorter, reduced version. This is why in software, a stub is considered temporary: it's a stand-in until the real thing is built. And in everyday life, a pencil stub is what you use when you can't find a proper pencil. There's a mild sense of "this is not ideal, but it'll do."

That feeling — the small, blunt, leftover piece that makes do — is the soul of the word.
